tip: 'Ojalá' is fossilized Arabic – 'law sha Allah', if God wills. It's a leftover prayer, so it always takes subjunctive: 'ojalá haga', never 'hace'.
'Para' + infinitive only works when subjects match. New actor doing the goal? Switch to 'para que' + subjunctive: the air, not you, does the entering – 'para que entre'.
'Salga', not 'sale' – this flight may not exist yet. Hunting for something unfound? Its description takes subjunctive. A found flight 'que sale' would be indicative.
'Tocar' (to touch) doubles as 'to be one's turn': the chore touches you. 'Nos toca limpiar' – cleaning lands on us. The task is the subject; you're just its target.
'Se comenta' = 'it's being said' – the 'se' erases the speaker entirely. Spanish's favorite way to pass along gossip without naming who's talking.
'Lleva esperándola' – she 'carries' waiting? 'Llevar' + '-ndo' measures how long something has been going on: carrying a whole week of waiting, no 'has been' needed.
'Antes de que' always takes subjunctive: 'lleguen'.
'Es mejor que' is a judgment, not a fact – so 'lleguemos' goes subjunctive. Arriving early is being recommended, not reported as actually happening.
'El proyecto' comes first for emphasis – but front an object and Spanish demands an echo pronoun: that 'lo' re-marks the project so nobody reads it as the subject.
'Pasar' for what's happening: '¿Qué te pasa?' = What's wrong with you? / What's happening to you? Indirect object marks the affected person.
'Ve' here is 'go!' (from 'ir') – but 've' is also the command for 'ver', 'see!'. Only context decides which; the supermarket destination settles it here.
'Necesitar que' + subjunctive: needing someone else to act. 'Necesito que me ayudes' (I need you to help me).
'Seguir sin' + infinitive = still haven't / still can't.
'Haga lo que haga' is literally 'may he do what he may do' – twin subjunctives sandwiching 'lo que' is Spanish's formula for 'whatever / no matter what'.
'El abrigo', not 'tu abrigo' – with clothes and body parts, the reflexive 'ponte' already says whose it is, so Spanish uses plain 'el' where English insists on 'your'.
'Por si' (in case) skips the subjunctive you'd expect: plain 'hace', not 'haga'. Spanish treats the just-in-case scenario as real enough to state flatly.
'Se lo voy a mandar': 'le' + 'lo' would clash, so 'le' becomes 'se' before 'lo'.
Where English summons the devil, Spanish summons 'el rey de Roma' – the king of Rome. Same magic: name someone and they appear. No actual royalty involved.
'Me alegra que' + subjunctive – expressing emotion about something.
The shop really is closing – yet 'esté' is subjunctive. 'Es una lástima que' frames your reaction to a fact, and reactions take subjunctive even when the fact is true.
'Está fría' – 'está' flags a state the soup got into: it went cold, so you can fix it. 'Es fría' would describe gazpacho, cold by design and beyond rescuing.
'Encontrarás' is the true future tense – Spanish saves it for predictions and promises like this one, while everyday plans usually get 'voy a' + verb.
English pulls legs; Spanish grabs hair: 'tomé el pelo' = I teased or fooled him. Different body part, same gentle deception.
False friend alert: 'suspendí el examen' means I FAILED it, not postponed it. A suspended exam in Spain is a flunked one; to postpone, you want 'aplazar'.
English says 'if you would have asked' – Spanish never puts conditional after 'si'. The if-half takes 'hubieras pedido'; 'habría' lives only in the result half.
'Sin que' (without) + subjunctive. Always triggers subjunctive.
'El quinto pino' – the fifth pine – is Spanish for the middle of nowhere, after a real row of pines on old Madrid's edge; the fifth was a long hike out.
'No es que' + subjunctive, 'sino que' + indicative = it's not that... but rather...
'Por muy' + adjective + 'que' + subjunctive = however much.
'Dámelo' stacks 'da' + 'me' + 'lo' in fixed order: person before thing, always 'me lo', never 'lo me'. The written accent keeps the stress where plain 'da' had it.
